title: Positioning & brand promise
summary: Conduit’s observed public position is hospitality AI agents that answer guests, act in connected tools, and coordinate the work that follows—not a generic chatbot. This guide separates that language from a recommended buyer-facing promise, attaches named proof without treating it as a typical result, and lists claims that should stay out of guarantees.
markdown:
## Core positioning

**Observed company language.** The shortest public line is “AI agents for hospitality.” The homepage expands it: answer guest messages and calls, handle requests end to end, and coordinate work across teams. The company page calls Conduit “the AI agent platform for hospitality”: a fleet of on-brand agents across every channel that convert inquiries into bookings, drive upsell revenue, run internal operations, and surface insights, connected to systems operators already use. The manifesto uses a sharper frame—“the coordination layer for hospitality”—an agent that works the same channels an operator does and acts on the business’s behalf instead of only shuttling messages. Industry nav is short-term rentals, independent hotels, and hotel groups. The product system behind that claim is [AI Agents](#knowledge/product-agents), [Inbox](#knowledge/product-inbox), [Guest Portals](#knowledge/product-portals), and [Workflows](#knowledge/product-workflows), with Operations labeled coming soon. Identity, founding-year, and brand-count conflicts belong in [Company overview](#knowledge/company-overview); capability packaging belongs in [Product catalog & capability map](#knowledge/products-capabilities). [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/company) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/manifesto)

**Recommended articulation (draft, not a published slogan).** For a guest-operations buyer: Conduit is the hospitality-specific agent layer that answers guests on the channels they already use, takes the next step in connected tools, and hands exceptions to your team with the thread intact. Keep manifesto “coordination layer” language for thought leadership. Keep “AI agents for hospitality” for awareness. Do not invent a new category name.

## Promise and supporting pillars

**Observed promise.** Agents answer with property information and reservation data, act through connected tools (for example updating a booking, collecting payment, or creating a task), and escalate when a person is needed. Inbox brings messages and calls into one workspace with history. Portals give guests one branded stay link for arrival details, extras, payment, and an AI concierge. Workflows schedule confirmations, check-in, follow-ups, and rule-based upgrades. Homepage supporting claims include multilingual replies, inspectable agent activity, scheduled workflows, and reporting on automation rate, response time, resolution, and guest satisfaction. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/agents) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/inbox) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/portals) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/workflows) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/)

| Pillar (observed) | What a guest-ops team gets | What not to inflate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answer | Voice and chat across email, WhatsApp, OTAs, social, phone | Coverage depends on connected accounts |
| Act | Booking context, procedures you set, tasks and payments in supported tools | A logo is not a write-back guarantee |
| Coordinate | One inbox, handoffs with history, team notes | Humans still own exceptions |
| Journey | Workflows plus Portals for pre-arrival, extras, follow-up | Portals are packaged separately on the public site |

**Recommended promise (draft).** Lead with the job: catch the 1 a.m. lockout, keep the booking next to the message, and let the agent run the routine so people handle the work that needs judgment. Attach one named story from [Customer evidence & usable proof](#knowledge/customer-evidence). Do not convert “end to end” into a guarantee that every request closes without a human.

## Why this work matters

The manifesto’s commercial argument is that hospitality already solved message speed; the bottleneck is how fast a person can absorb volume and act, especially after hours and across inboxes that do not talk to each other. It illustrates with attributed customer data: median human response on one team ranged from 26 minutes to 46 hours, versus an agent answer in 93 seconds. Hiring VAs is framed as adding people to orchestration, not removing it. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/manifesto)

Named stories make that concrete without treating them as typical. Haven reports moving from about 40% to 90% automation across roughly 270 properties, with support need falling from about 25 people to two per shift after teaching workflows. HomeHop reports growing from 40 to 108 listings without extra guest-support hires. Cascadia reports absorbing a first property-management acquisition without hiring more guest-service staff. Lauderdale reports support cost falling from $4,000 to $600 per month and average response from 57 minutes to 2 minutes. Those are Conduit-attributed outcomes, not a rate card. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/haven-2026) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/homehop) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/cascadia-getaways) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/lauderdale-hotel)

Recommended emphasis in commercial copy: growth without linear headcount, after-hours coverage, and one thread for guest plus booking—not “AI changes everything.”

## Reasons to believe

| Type | Usable as | How to say it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product | Agents, Inbox, Portals, Workflows as named surfaces; voice plus messaging; procedures and escalation | Point at product pages; do not treat Operations as the current catalog |
| Named proof | Haven, HomeHop, Cascadia, Lauderdale, Wynwood, Bocobay, Cosmica, Canbnb, Flex, Bali/Easy BnB | One story, one metric, caveat in the same sentence |
| Company-reported scale | Homepage 300+ brands in 120+ countries; manifesto 50M+ conversations, $3B+ reservation value influenced, 87% autonomous resolution, 95% CSAT | Attribute as company reporting; LinkedIn says “over 1000+” brands—do not reconcile in the same asset |
| Security | Homepage SOC 2 Type II, enterprise controls, HIPAA-workflow language | Company-reported in this corpus, not a third-party letter |
| G2 widget | 4.7 / 5 | Site citation only |

[Source](https://www.conduit.ai/) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/manifesto) [Source](https://www.linkedin.com/company/useconduitai/)

## Positioning boundaries

Stay inside hospitality guest operations (the three published industries, plus FAQ language for serviced-apartment operators). Do not pitch Conduit as a PMS, channel manager, generic helpdesk, or a substitute for people on the property. Operations is “coming soon” in the product nav even where stories mention maintenance or cleaning workflows—do not sell the coming-soon SKU as generally available. Do not promise 90% automation, $500k asset value, or 87% resolution as expected results. Do not use conflicting brand counts in one asset. Bocobay’s Intercom move and Flex’s decision not to rebuild conversational AI are named displacements, not proof that Conduit beats every competitor on the “Conduit vs.” list. For wording rules see [Brand voice & language](#knowledge/brand-voice) and [Audience-to-message map](#knowledge/message-map).
open_questions: Which brand-count line (homepage 300+ vs LinkedIn 1000+) is approved for external copy, and should manifesto scale metrics stay thought-leadership only?
Is Operations still a positioning boundary as “coming soon,” or may maintenance/housekeeping language from stories and Full Suite packaging be used as current product?
What hotel-group proof, if any, can sit beside STR and boutique-hotel stories without stretching Lauderdale or Wynwood?
